items.claim: A value that reaches a page only through a client-side template's escaped interpolation or attribute binding is not XSS, because the framework assigns it through textContent/setAttribute rather than by string-concatenating it into markup.
items.body: The classic false positive is a reflected parameter that appears un-escaped in a raw HTTP response body but is in fact passed through a template engine that escapes it before insertion. Vue makes the mechanism explicit: interpolation of a user string yields escaped output, and the escaping is done with native browser APIs rather than string surgery, so a payload that closes a tag or adds an event handler is neutralised by the assignment itself. A hunter who reads the raw response and concludes 'the tag is unescaped, therefore XSS' is reading a pre-template artefact. The field test is to determine whether the value's final insertion goes through a text node or attribute assignment, or through an HTML-string sink; only the latter is a finding. Note the corollary: the same framework is unsafe the moment the value reaches a sink that takes an HTML string.
items.disproof: The rule is wrong the moment the value is also passed to a raw-HTML sink on the same render path (v-html, innerHTML, a markdown-to-HTML renderer, a server-side {{ triple-brace or |safe filter) - the framework's escaping applies only to the escaped bindings, and one raw sink is enough. It is also wrong if the value is echoed into a context the template engine does not own at all, such as a JSON blob later read by another script and written to a sink, or a value concatenated into an inline <script> block. Finally it is wrong if the app is not the framework it appears to be on some route - a JSON API or a server-rendered fragment served outside the template engine lands the string in raw HTML.

sources.quote: This escaping is done using native browser APIs, like textContent , so a vulnerability can only exist if the browser itself is vulnerable.
As a second step, it is good practice to escape all output of the application , especially when re-displaying user input, which hasn't been input-filtered

items.claim: Injection that survives a server-side markup-to-HTML renderer (Markdown, Textile, wiki syntax) but never reaches a script-execution context in the delivered page is a content-injection issue, not XSS, and must not be reported as XSS without a browser-confirmed execution trace.
items.body:
Server-side markup renderers are a classic source of XSS false positives, because the renderer's output is visibly full of angle brackets and the injection is obvious in the raw HTML. But a renderer that escapes or strips the dangerous constructs produces inert markup: the tag text is present in the response, and no script runs. Rails' own security guide is candid that a renderer such as RedCloth is itself vulnerable, and separately that a permitted-list sanitiser plus output escaping is what actually stops the injection - the point being that the renderer's transformation is a stage, not the sink. The hunter's job is to identify the second stage: which script, handler, or navigation consumes this markup, and whether it is reachable. A wiki comment rendered to escaped

and is a formatting bug; the same comment reaching a profile field rendered as raw HTML, or a client that reads the same field into innerHTML, is XSS.
items.disproof: The rule collapses when the rendered markup is later consumed by a sink: a client-side viewer that fetches the same field and assigns it to innerHTML, a print/export pipeline that re-injects it, an email client that renders it, or a second page that echoes the raw stored value. It is also wrong if the renderer emits script-capable constructs by design - raw HTML passthrough, a custom block that permits <iframe>, inline event handlers, or javascript: links - in which case the renderer's own output is the sink and the injection is XSS. And a payload confirmed executing in a real browser, with a second observable such as a network beacon, is XSS by definition regardless of which stage introduced it.

sources.quote: If you want to provide text formatting other than HTML (due to security), use a mark-up language which is converted to HTML on the server-side.
User-provided HTML can never be considered 100% safe unless it's in a sandboxed iframe or in a part of the app where only the user who wrote that HTML can ever be exposed to it.

items.claim: A filter that only deletes the literal string "script" from user input is not a control at all: the surrounding angle brackets survive, so the injected tag remains well-formed and still executes.
items.body: This is the canonical example of why deny-lists fail, and it is worth internalising as a validation reflex: whenever a report says the app 'filters out script tags', check what the filter removes. A keyword-level delete leaves the '<' and '>' untouched, so the payload assembles itself after the filter runs. Rails documents the failure and the fix together: permitted-list filtering states the values allowed, and restricted lists are never complete. In the field this changes what you test - you do not conclude 'the app strips script tags, so no XSS'; you inject a split-tag payload and see whether the filter operates on the tag name, the whole element, or a substring. Note the deeper trap: a permitted-list sanitiser can still be incomplete if the allow-list itself includes a dangerous attribute or URL scheme.
items.disproof: The rule is false if the filter is a real parser-based sanitiser rather than a substring delete - a tokenising HTML sanitiser that rebuilds the document from a permitted list of elements and attributes neutralises the split-tag payload because the brackets are consumed as part of a rejected tag, not left orphaned. It is also false if a downstream layer re-encodes or re-parses, or if the filter strips all angle brackets rather than a keyword. And the rule is only about the filter: if the value is separately output-escaped at render time, the split payload is inert regardless of what the filter did.

sources.quote: Permitted list filtering states the values allowed as opposed to the values not allowed. Restricted lists are never complete.
Perform input validation when handling data from external storage as you would with data from any untrusted source.

items.claim: A reflected XSS on a page whose CSP is nonce-based is only exploitable if the injected markup executes on that same page and inherits its policy; a payload delivered on a page with no CSP header, or a different policy, is not covered by the nonce argument.
items.body: Nonce-based CSP is a strong control and it is also the most common reason a confirmed-looking XSS report gets closed. The mechanism is that the policy names one specific inline script by hash of a per-response random value, and every other inline script without that value is refused. CSP3's 'strict-dynamic' source expression extends this: it trusts script which already executes to load more script via non-parser-inserted script elements, so an attacker who gets one nonce-bearing script in still wins - which is why nonce policies are judged on whether the nonce itself is injectable. The hunter's obligation is to state precisely which header and which document the proof ran under. A payload echoed by an API endpoint with no CSP, or by an error page, or by a file-serve route, inherits no nonce and no policy - the 'CSP blocks it' closure only holds for the exact response you observed the header on. Report the header verbatim alongside the request and response pair.
items.disproof: The claim is false if the policy uses 'strict-dynamic' together with a host allow-list, because a single executed script then loads arbitrary further script without needing the nonce again. It is also false if the nonce value is itself attacker-influenced - reflected in the page, derived from a predictable or reused value, or set on a script the attacker controls - since the whole policy then collapses to allowing that script. And a policy that omits default-src or leaves script-src unset inherits the permissive default, so no nonce is being enforced in the first place. Finally the argument is void if the vulnerable response carries no Content-Security-Policy header at all.

sources.quote: The 'strict-dynamic' source expression will now allow script which executes on a page to load more script via non- "parser-inserted" script elements.
In any web application, allowing unsanitized, user-provided content to be executed as HTML, CSS, or JavaScript is potentially dangerous, so it should be avoided wherever possible.
